title: s. 138 notice received on a cheque given as security, not against a debt

input.text: Received this by RPAD yesterday. Notice dated 18.11.2026 from advocate for one Suresh Purohit. Says my cheque of Rs 4,50,000 dated 02.09.2026 was dishonoured, memo attached, demands payment in 15 days. Cheque was given as SECURITY for a plot agreement that fell through — no debt was due on 02.09.2026. I have the agreement. Do I reply or wait? What happens if I don't?

drafts.title: Reply to s. 138 Notice — Security Cheque Defence
drafts.body:
SYNTHETIC / DEMO — gate-shaped worked example; NOT filing-ready. [PENDING] holes are deliberate.

LEGAL NOTICE — REPLY TO NOTICE DATED 18.11.2026 UNDER s. 138, NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS ACT, 1881

To: [Advocate for Mr. Suresh Purohit, Jodhpur]
From: Advocate for the Noticee

Sub: Reply to your notice dated 18.11.2026 re cheque of Rs 4,50,000 dated 02.09.2026

1. Without admitting any liability, this replies to your notice dated 18.11.2026, received by the reply-writer on [PENDING — exact RPAD receipt date to be fixed from the cover].

2. The cheque for Rs 4,50,000 dated 02.09.2026 was not issued toward any debt. It was handed as SECURITY under an agreement to sell that fell through. The agreement is on record.

3. The statutory presumption under s. 139, NI Act 1881 is rebuttable. No legally enforceable liability subsisted on 02.09.2026, and my client puts your client to strict proof of such liability on the date of presentation.

4. Your client's remedy, if any, is to sue on the agreement, not to invoke s. 138, NI Act 1881.

5. The agreement produced is unstamped; it is relied on subject to the law on impounding.

6. The proposition that a security cheque can still ground s. 138 where an enforceable liability exists at presentation is contested, and no authority is cited here. [PENDING — a named judgment with a paragraph on s. 138/139 and security cheques must be verified before it is pleaded.]

7. My client reserves all rights. Reply under proviso (b) to s. 138, NI Act 1881 is hereby given within the statutory period from receipt.

Place: Jodhpur    Date: [PENDING — dispatch date]

For the Noticee

terminalOutcome.label: Send the reply, but supervisor review the 'security' framing before dispatch
terminalOutcome.rationale: The reply window is a hard statutory clock. Missing it forfeits a right that cannot be recovered later. But 'it was a security cheque' is a defence of contested strength, so the framing needs a human before it goes out.
terminalOutcome.nextAction: Fix the receipt date from the cover, settle the reply, dispatch by RPAD, and diary the date on which a complaint may be filed.

teachingNotes: 'Do I reply or wait?' is the beginner's default question on every s. 138 notice. Waiting is only safe when the receipt date is far off. Here it is not.
The statutory reply is not an admission document. Its job is to create the record of the defence and to preserve the right to be heard on it.

A security cheque is not an automatic acquittal. The live question is whether an enforceable liability existed when the cheque was presented — which is why the cancellation correspondence matters more than the word 'security'.
The unstamped agreement is a trap: it may need impounding, and an advocate who waves it around at the reply stage without noticing looks careless.
commonMistakes: Computing the reply period from the notice date instead of the receipt date.
Writing a bare 'the cheque was given as security' with no factual scaffolding.
Discarding the RPAD cover, which destroys the receipt-date proof.
Admitting the signature and the debt in the same sentence as denying liability.
seniorVariants: Reply without either admitting or denying the debt: state the agreement, the security purpose, the failure of consideration, and put the complainant to proof of a subsisting liability on the presentation date.
Call for the complainant's ledger and the presentation particulars.
Flag the unstamped agreement and pre-empt the impounding objection.
Diary the one-month complaint window from the day after the reply period ends, and prepare the accused's s. 145 NI Act evidence in advance.

accuracy.adverseFact: If the agreement to sell provided for forfeiture of the earnest money on the buyer's default, part of the cheque amount may well be due — the security defence then narrows to the excess rather than the whole sum.
